{{Short description|Geometric structure on a smooth manifold}}
In the mathematical field of [[differential geometry]], an '''almost-contact structure''' is a certain kind of geometric structure on a [[smooth manifold]], obtained by combining a [[contact structure|contact-element structure]] (not necessarily a contact structure) and an [[almost-complex structure]]. They can be considered as an odd-dimensional counterpart to [[Almost complex manifold|almost complex manifolds]]. 

They were introduced by John Gray in 1959.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gray |first=John W. |date=1959 |title=Some Global Properties of Contact Structures |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1970192 |journal=Annals of Mathematics |volume=69 |issue=2 |pages=421–450 |doi=10.2307/1970192 |issn=0003-486X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[Shigeo Sasaki]] in 1960 introduced [[Sasakian manifold]] to study them.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sasaki |first=Shigeo |date=1960 |title=On differentiable manifolds with certain structures which are closely related to almost contact structure, I |journal=Tohoku Mathematical Journal |series=2 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=459–476 |doi=10.2748/tmj/1178244407|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Definition ==
Given a smooth manifold <math>M</math>, an almost-contact structure is a triple <math>(Q, J, \xi)</math> of a [[Distribution (differential geometry)|hyperplane distribution]] <math>Q</math>, an [[almost-complex structure]] <math>J</math> on <math>Q</math>, and a [[vector field]] <math>\xi</math> which is [[Transversality|transverse]] to <math>Q</math>. That is, for each point <math>p</math> of <math>M</math>, one selects a contact element (that is, a codimension-one [[linear subspace]] <math>Q_p</math> of the [[tangent space]] <math>T_p M</math>), a [[linear complex structure]] on it (that is, a linear function <math>J_p : Q_p \to Q_p</math> such that <math>J_p \circ J_p = - \operatorname{id}_{Q_p}</math>), and an element <math>\xi_p</math> of <math>T_p M</math> which is not contained in <math>Q_p</math>. As usual, the selection must be smooth.<ref name=":1">{{cite book |last=Blair |first=David E. |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-8176-4959-3 |title=Riemannian Geometry of Contact and Symplectic Manifolds |date=2010 |publisher=Birkhäuser |isbn=978-0-8176-4958-6 |edition=2nd |series=Progress in Mathematics |location=Boston, MA |pages=343 |language=en |chapter=4. Associated Metrics |volume=203 |doi=10.1007/978-0-8176-4959-3 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-0-8176-4959-3_4}}</ref>

Equivalently, one may define an almost-contact structure as a triple <math>(\xi, \eta, \phi)</math>, where <math>\xi</math> is a vector field on <math>M</math>, <math>\eta</math> is a [[One-form (differential geometry)|1-form]] on <math>M</math>, and <math>\phi</math> is a [[Tensor field|(1,1)-tensor field]] on <math>M</math>, such that they satisfy the two conditions<math display="block">\phi^2=-\mathrm{id}+\eta \otimes \xi, \quad \eta(\xi)=1 .</math>Or in more detail, for any <math>p \in M</math> and any <math>v \in T_p M</math>,
* <math>\eta_p(v) \xi_p = \phi_p \circ \phi_p(v) + v</math>
* <math>\eta_p(\xi_p) = 1</math>
Because the choice of the transverse vector field <math>\xi</math> is smooth, the field <math>\xi</math> is a '''co-orientation''' of the distribution of contact elements <math>Q</math>.

More abstractly, it can be defined as a [[G-structure on a manifold|G-structure]] obtained by [[reduction of the structure group]] from <math>GL(2n+1)</math> to <math>U(n) \times 1</math>.

=== Equivalence ===
In one direction, given <math>(\xi, J, Q)</math>, one can define for each <math>p</math> in <math>M</math> a linear map <math>\eta_p : T_p M \to \R</math> and a linear map <math>\phi_p : T_p M \to T_p M</math> by<math display="block">\begin{align}
\eta_p(u)&=0\text{ if }u\in Q_p\\
\eta_p(\xi_p)&=1\\
\phi_p(u)&=J_p(u)\text{ if }u\in Q_p\\
\phi_p(\xi)&=0.
\end{align}</math>and one can check directly, by decomposing <math>v</math> relative to the [[direct sum]] decomposition <math>T_p M = Q_p \oplus \left\{ k \xi_p : k \in \R \right\}</math>, that<math display="block">\begin{align}
\eta_p(v) \xi_p &= \phi_p \circ \phi_p(v) + v
\end{align}</math>for any <math>v</math> in <math>T_p M</math>.

In another direction, given <math>(\xi, \eta, \phi)</math>, one can define <math>Q_p</math> to be the [[Kernel (linear algebra)|kernel]] of the linear map <math>\eta_p</math>, and one can check that the restriction of <math>\phi_p</math> to <math>Q_p</math> is valued in <math>Q_p</math>, thereby defining <math>J_p</math>.

=== Properties ===
Given an almost contact structure on a <math>(2n+1)</math>-manifold, we have:<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|location=Theorem 4.1}}

* <math>\phi \xi = 0</math>
* <math>\eta \circ \phi = 0</math>
* <math>\phi</math> has rank ''2n''.

== Relation to other manifolds ==

=== Metric ===
Given an almost-contact manifold equipped with the previously defined <math>(Q, J, \xi, \eta, \phi)</math>, we may add a [[Riemannian metric]] <math>g</math> to it. We say the metric is compatible with the almost-contact structure iff the metric satisfies the metric ''compatibility'' condition:<math display="block">g(\phi X, \phi Y)=g(X, Y)-\eta(X) \eta(Y) \quad \text { for all } X, Y \in \Gamma(T M) .</math>Such a manifold is called an '''almost contact metric manifold'''.<ref name=":1" />

Define the fundamental 2-form <math display="inline">\Phi</math> by <math display="inline">\Phi(X, Y)=g(X, \phi Y)</math>. Then <math display="inline">\Phi</math> is skew-symmetric and <math display="inline">\eta(X)= g(X, \xi)</math>.

Compatible metrics are easy to find. That is, they are not [[Rigidity (mathematics)|rigid]]. To construct one, take any metric <math display="inline">k^{\prime}</math>, and let <math display="inline">k(X, Y)=k^{\prime}\left(\phi^2 X, \phi^2 Y\right)+\eta(X) \eta(Y)</math>, then this is a compatible metric:<math display="block">
g(X, Y)=\frac{1}{2}(k(X, Y)+k(\phi X, \phi Y)+\eta(X) \eta(Y))
</math>Special cases used in the literature are:

* Contact metric manifold: additionally <math display="inline">\eta \wedge(d \eta)^n \neq 0</math> and <math display="inline">d \eta=2 \Phi</math>.
* [[Sasakian manifold]]: contact metric manifold, with normality condition <math display="inline">N_{\phi}+2 d \eta \otimes \xi=0</math>.
* Almost coKähler manifold: almost contact metric, with <math display="inline">d \eta=0</math> and <math display="inline">d \Phi=0</math> (normality not assumed).

==== Classification ====
They have been fully classified via group representation theory into 4096 classes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chinea |first=D. |last2=Gonzalez |first2=C. |date=1990-12-01 |title=A classification of almost contact metric manifolds |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01766972 |journal=Annali di Matematica Pura ed Applicata |language=en |volume=156 |issue=1 |pages=15–36 |doi=10.1007/BF01766972 |issn=1618-1891}}</ref>

Let <math display="inline">(\phi, \xi, \eta, g)</math> be an almost contact metric structure on a <math display="inline">(2 n+1)</math>-manifold, and let <math display="inline">\Phi(X, Y)= g(X, \phi Y)</math>. At each point, regard<math display="block">
T:=\nabla \Phi \in C(V) \subset \otimes^3 T^* M,
</math>where <math display="block">\begin{aligned}
C(V)=\{a \mid a(X, Y, Z)&=-a(X, Z, Y), \\ 
a(X, \phi Y, \phi Z)&=-a(X, Y, Z)+ \eta(Y) a(X, \xi, Z)+\eta(Z) a(X, Y, \xi)\}
\end{aligned}</math>For <math display="inline">n>2</math>, it splits into orthogonal, irreducible, <math display="inline">U(n) \times 1</math>-invariant subspaces<math display="block">
C(V)=C_1 \oplus C_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus C_{12} .
</math>An almost contact metric manifold is of class <math display="inline">U \subset \bigoplus_{i=1}^{12} C_i</math> if <math display="inline">T_x \in U</math> for all <math display="inline">x</math>. Hence there are <math display="inline">2^{12}</math> classes.

Given such a manifold, it can be classified as follows: compute <math display="inline">\nabla \Phi</math>, project it onto the twelve <math display="inline">C_i</math> (via the formulas in Table III of the paper), and identify the class by which <math display="inline">C_i</math> components are nonzero.

Specific cases named in the literature:

* Cosymplectic: <math display="inline">U=\{0\}(d \eta=0, d \Phi=0, \nabla \Phi=0)</math>.
* Nearly <math display="inline">K</math>-cosymplectic: <math display="inline">U=C_1</math>.
* Almost cosymplectic: <math display="inline">U=C_2 \oplus C_9</math>.
* <math display="inline">\alpha</math>-Kenmotsu: <math display="inline">U=C_5</math>.
* <math display="inline">\alpha</math>-Sasakian: <math display="inline">U=C_6</math>.
* Trans-Sasakian <math display="inline">(\alpha, \beta): U=C_5 \oplus C_6</math>.
* Quasi-Sasakian: <math display="inline">U=C_6 \oplus C_7</math>.

== Examples ==
A '''cosymplectic structure''' on a smooth manifold of dimension <math>2n+1</math> induces an almost-contact structure.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Cappelletti-Montano |first1=Beniamino |last2=De Nicola |first2=Antonio |last3=Yudin |first3=Ivan |date=November 2013 |title=A survey on cosymplectic geometry |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0129055X13430022 |journal=Reviews in Mathematical Physics |volume=25 |issue=10 |pages=1343002 |doi=10.1142/S0129055X13430022 |arxiv=1305.3704 |bibcode=2013RvMaP..2543002C |hdl=10316/47481 |issn=0129-055X}}</ref> Specifically, a cosymplectic structure is a tuple <math>(\eta, \omega)</math> where <math>\eta</math> is a closed 1-form, <math>\omega</math> is a closed 2-form, and <math>\eta \wedge \omega^n \neq 0</math> at every point. One way to produce a cosymplectic structure is by foliating the manifold into symplectic manifolds, and set <math>\omega</math> to be the symplectic structure on each manifold, and have <math>\ker\eta</math> parallel to the tangent planes through the foliation.<ref>{{cite book |last=Blair |first=David E. |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-8176-4959-3 |title=Riemannian Geometry of Contact and Symplectic Manifolds |date=2010 |publisher=Birkhäuser |isbn=978-0-8176-4958-6 |edition=2nd |series=Progress in Mathematics |location=Boston, MA |pages=343 |language=en |chapter=6. Sasakian and Cosymplectic Manifolds |volume=203 |doi=10.1007/978-0-8176-4959-3 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-0-8176-4959-3_6 }}</ref>

Another common way to construct a cosymplectic structure is through time-dependent [[Hamiltonian mechanics]]. Let a phase space be <math>M</math>. A trajectory of a system in phase space is a path in <math>\R \times M</math>. Let <math>p, q</math> be canonical coordinates on the phase space, which may be allowed to vary over time. Then <math>\theta := \sum_i p_i dq_i, \; \omega := d\theta, \; \eta := dt</math> provides is an almost-contact structure on the manifold <math>\R \times M</math>.

The construction of the almost-contact metric structure:<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Theorem 3.3}}

* <math display="inline">Q=\operatorname{ker} \eta</math> (a rank- <math display="inline">2 n</math> distribution).
* The Reeb field <math display="inline">\xi</math> by <math display="inline">\eta(\xi)=1</math> and <math display="inline">\iota_{\xi} \omega=0</math> (uniquely determined because <math display="inline">\eta \wedge \omega^n \neq 0</math> ).
* Since <math display="inline">\left.\omega\right|_Q</math> is symplectic, choose an orientation of <math>Q</math> consistent with <math>\omega^n</math>. Then pick any almost-complex structure <math display="inline">J</math> on <math display="inline">Q</math> that is <math display="inline">\omega</math>-compatible. In detail, it must satisfy <math display="inline">J^2=-\mathrm{id}</math> on <math display="inline">Q</math>, <math display="inline">\omega(\cdot, J \cdot)</math> is a positive-definite bilinear form, and <math display="inline">\omega(J \cdot, J \cdot) = \omega</math>.
** Explicitly, if <math>\R^{2n}</math> has symplectic form <math>\omega = \sum_{i=1}^n dp_i \wedge dq_i</math>, then <math>(q, p) \mapsto (-p, q)</math> is a <math display="inline">\omega</math>-compatible complex form on it.
* Set <math display="inline">\left.\phi\right|_Q=J</math> and <math display="inline">\phi(\xi)=0</math>.

To show it, note that<math display="block">
\eta(\xi)=1, \quad \eta \circ \phi=0,\left.\quad \phi^2\right|_Q=J^2=-\mathrm{id}_Q, \quad \phi^2(\xi)=0 .
</math>Thus <math display="inline">\phi^2=-\mathrm{id}+\eta \otimes \xi</math> on all of <math display="inline">T M</math>. Hence <math display="inline">(\xi, \eta, \phi)</math> is an almost-contact structure.
